passage: Through the thin wall of the flat in Toa Payoh, Wei could hear Ma and Ba arguing again, low and fast, about the rent. Her maths test was in her bag: 68 out of 100. They had argued last week too, the night her report book came home. So it was her. It had to be. She took out the test and redid every wrong question in neat pencil, then lined up all the shoes by the door. 'What are you doing?' her big sister Xin whispered. 'If I'm perfect, they'll stop.' Xin climbed onto the bunk beside her. 'They're arguing about the rent, Wei. Not you.' Next morning Xin told Ma, and Ma pulled Wei onto her lap before school. 'Grown-up worries. Not yours. Never yours.'

qa.q: What did Wei score in the maths test?
qa.a: Wei scored 68 out of 100.

qa.q: Why does Wei believe the argument is her fault?
qa.a: Wei feels guilty and worried because the parents argued the night her report book came home, so linking the two seems obvious and being perfect feels like a way to fix it.

qa.q: What choice by Xin made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Xin told Wei the real reason and then told Ma the next morning, so a parent could reassure Wei directly that grown-up worries are not hers.

qa.q: How might Ma feel on hearing what Wei said?
qa.a: Ma would likely feel sad and protective 🤍 that Wei was carrying the blame, which is why she pulls Wei onto her lap before school.

grounding: Shows a child who believes her parents' arguments are caused by her marks and tries to be perfect, until her sister and mother make clear it is not her fault.

passage: In the school counsellor's room, Madhav sat on the edge of the blue chair and explained his plan. 'I'm going to get full marks in every test. And not make noise. And finish my whole dabba.' Shankar sir asked why. Madhav looked at his shoes. 'Because Mummy and Papa fight when my marks are bad. Last Sunday they fought after my Hindi test. If I'm perfect, they won't.' Shankar sir waited. 'What were they talking about when they fought?' Madhav thought. 'Papa's office. And Nani's house.' 'Did anyone say your Hindi test?' A long pause. 'No.' 'Grown-ups argue about grown-up things.' Madhav wasn't sure. Shankar sir asked if he could call Madhav's mother, so she could tell him herself. Madhav nodded.

qa.q: What were Madhav's parents talking about when they fought?
qa.a: They were talking about Papa's office and Nani's house.

qa.q: Why does Madhav plan to be perfect?
qa.a: Madhav believes his bad marks cause the fights, so being perfect feels like the only way to keep home peaceful and gives him a sense of control.

qa.q: Which question from Shankar sir helped Madhav look again?
qa.a: 'What were they talking about when they fought?' let Madhav notice from his own memory that the topic was Papa's office and Nani's house, not his test.

qa.q: What might Madhav's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: She may feel sad and surprised that Madhav has been blaming himself, and want to reassure him clearly herself.

grounding: Shows a child who believes his parents fight because of his marks and plans to be perfect, and a counsellor who helps him look at the facts and involves his mother.

passage: I'm Chandrika, from the flat across the landing, and I've known Amandeep since he was born. These past weeks I've heard raised voices from his parents' flat most evenings, only voices. And I've noticed Amandeep changing. He used to leave his cycle anywhere; now it's parked perfectly straight. He brings my newspaper up from the stairs every morning before I ask. Yesterday he showed me his notebook, every page with a star, and said very seriously, 'If I get all stars, there'll be no shouting.' I don't know exactly what goes on in his head. But I think he believes it's his job to fix it. I told him, 'Grown-ups shouting is never a child's fault.' Then I knocked on his mother's door and told her what he'd said.

qa.q: What did Amandeep show Chandrika yesterday?
qa.a: Amandeep showed Chandrika his notebook, every page with a star.

qa.q: What does 'If I get all stars, there'll be no shouting' suggest Amandeep believes?
qa.a: It suggests Amandeep feels anxious and responsible, believing the shouting is his fault and that being perfect will stop it, which is why he parks his cycle so straight.

qa.q: Which of Chandrika's two actions matters more, and why?
qa.a: Telling his mother matters most, because a parent can reassure Amandeep directly and see how the arguments are affecting him; Chandrika's words to him are a kind start.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's mother feel hearing what he said?
qa.a: She would likely feel worried and sad that he is carrying this, and may want to talk with him and keep grown-up arguments away from him.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a child who seems to believe his parents' arguments are his fault and tries to be perfect to stop them.

passage:
Monday: Sachin, nine, heard Mummy and Papa arguing in the kitchen, low and sharp, the same night his maths test came home with 12 out of 20. He lay in bed thinking: It's because of me. If I'd got 20, they wouldn't fight.

Wednesday: He made his bed without being asked, did his homework twice, and didn't laugh at cartoons in case the noise made things worse. When Papa sighed at the electricity bill, Sachin froze and quickly tidied the shoes.

Saturday: Mummy found him re-copying his test corrections at eleven at night. "Sachin, why are you still awake?"

"So you and Papa don't fight."

Tanuja sat on his bed. "Beta, listen. Papa and I argue about money and his long hours. Grown-up things. Never about you. It's not your job to fix it."

He wasn't sure he believed her. But he put the pencil down.

qa.q: What did Sachin's maths test come home with?
qa.a: 12 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Sachin freeze when Papa sighed at the electricity bill?
qa.a: Sachin believed the tension at home was his fault, so any sign of upset made him try harder to be perfect. He was scared his own behaviour could make things worse.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what could his parents keep doing?
qa.a: When Mummy found him up late and told him the arguments were about money and work, never about him. His parents could keep reassuring him, and try to keep arguments away from his hearing.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt learning why Sachin was awake at eleven?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt sad and a bit guilty that Sachin had been carrying their arguments. It likely made her want to protect him from that burden.

grounding: Over a week a boy believes his parents argue because of his marks and tries to be perfect, until his mother tells him the arguments are not about him.

passage:
Sarita, beta, you've been so quiet since your Mummy and Papa raised their voices last night. Come, sit with your Vijay Dadu.

When I was nine, in Jabalpur, my parents argued in the evenings. I was sure it was because of me. My report card was bad that year, and once they argued the same night it came. So I decided to be perfect. I polished everyone's shoes. I studied before sunrise. I even stopped playing marbles, in case my noise started a fight.

One night my Nani caught me studying by the lamp at midnight. I told her why. She held my face and said, "Their arguments are about money and your father's job. You didn't make them, and you can't fix them."

So, Sarita. Is it the same for you? You can tell me.

qa.q: What did Vijay Dadu stop playing, in case his noise started a fight?
qa.a: He stopped playing marbles.

qa.q: Why did young Vijay believe his parents' arguments were his fault?
qa.a: Young Vijay felt guilty and afraid; because his parents argued the same night his bad report card came, he linked the two and assumed he was the cause.

qa.q: Which choice of Vijay Dadu's makes it easier for Sarita to open up?
qa.a: He noticed Sarita's quietness, sat together with Sarita the very next day, and told his own story before gently asking if it's the same. That shows Sarita the feeling isn't unusual and invites talking.

qa.q: What might Sarita be feeling after the raised voices last night?
qa.a: Sarita may be worried and wondering whether the argument was somehow Sarita's fault, which could explain the quietness. Hearing Dadu's story may make it easier to say aloud.

grounding: A grandfather tells Sarita how, at nine, he believed his parents fought because of his marks and tried to be perfect, until his Nani reassured him.
